questions.problem: Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the $1$st term is $0$ and the $9$th term is $40.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by 

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

We already know that the first term is ${a}_{1}=0,$ so we just need to figure out the common difference $d.$ 

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms ${a}_{1}=0$ and ${a}_{9}=40$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{9}-{a}_{1}}{9-1} \\  & =\frac{40-0}{9-1} \\  & =\frac{40}{8} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence is  

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =0+(n-1)(5) \\  & =5n-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the general formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the $7$th term is $-18$ and the first term is $6.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is given by 

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

We already know that the first term is ${a}_{1}=6,$ so we just need to figure out the common difference $d.$ 

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms ${a}_{1}=6$ and ${a}_{7}=-18$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{7}-{a}_{1}}{7-1} \\  & =\frac{-18-6}{7-1} \\  & =\frac{-24}{6} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

So,  the formula for the $n$th term of our arithmetic sequence is  

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =6+(n-1)(-4) \\  & =6-4n+4 \\  & =10-4n.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The second and third terms of an arithmetic sequence are $45$ and $80,$ respectively. Determine the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence.
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by  

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,
$$

so we need to figure out the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$ 

Since the terms ${a}_{2}=45$ and ${a}_{3}=80$ are consecutive, we can subtract them to find the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{3}-{a}_{2} \\  & =80-45 \\  & =35\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, ${a}_{2}=45,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since ${a}_{2}$ is $1$ jump after ${a}_{1},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+1\cdot d \\ 45 & ={a}_{1}+35 \\ 45-35 & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =10\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence is:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =10+(n-1)\cdot 35 \\  & =10+35n-35 \\  & =35n-25\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The $7$th and $8$th terms of an arithmetic sequence are $-13$ and $-20,$ respectively. Determine the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence.
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by 

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,
$$

so we need to figure out the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$ 

Since the terms ${a}_{7}=-13$ and ${a}_{8}=-20$ are consecutive, we can subtract them to find the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{8}-{a}_{7} \\  & =-20-(-13) \\  & =-20+13 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, ${a}_{8}=-20,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since ${a}_{8}$ is $7$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{8} & ={a}_{1}+7d \\ -20 & ={a}_{1}+7(-7) \\ -20 & ={a}_{1}-49 \\ -20+49 & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =29+(n-1)(-7) \\  & =29-7n+7 \\  & =36-7n.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the $14$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the $3$rd term is $40$ and the $23$rd term is $-20.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,
$$

 
so we need to figure out the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms ${a}_{3}=40$ and ${a}_{23}=-20$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{23}-{a}_{3}}{23-3} \\  & =\frac{-20-40}{23-3} \\  & =\frac{(-60)}{20} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, ${a}_{3}=40,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since ${a}_{3}$ is $2$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}+2d \\ 40 & ={a}_{1}+2(-3) \\ 40 & ={a}_{1}-6 \\ 40+6 & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =46.\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =46+(n-1)(-3) \\  & =46-3n+3 \\  & =49-3n\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can find the $14$th term by substituting $n=14$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{14} & =49-3(14) \\  & =49-42 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the  $11$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the $19$th term is $99$ and the $4$th term is $-6.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by  

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,
$$

so we need to figure out the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms ${a}_{19}=99$ and ${a}_{4}=-6$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{19}-{a}_{4}}{19-4} \\  & =\frac{99-(-6)}{19-4} \\  & =\frac{105}{15} \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, ${a}_{4}=-6,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since ${a}_{4}$ is $3$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}+3d \\ -6 & ={a}_{1}+3\cdot 7 \\ -6 & ={a}_{1}+21 \\ {a}_{1} & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-27+(n-1)\cdot 7 \\  & =7n-34\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can find the $11$th term by substituting $n=11$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & =7(11)-34 \\  & =77-34 \\  & =43\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence given that the first term is $-1$ and the eighth term is $13.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by 

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d.
$$

We already know that the first term is $a_1=-1,$ so we just need to figure out the common difference $d.$

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms $a_1=-1$ and $a_8=13$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{8}-{a}_{1}}{8-1} \\  & =\frac{13-(-1)}{8-1} \\  & =\frac{14}{7} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence is  

$$
\eqalign{
		a_n&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
 		& = -1 + (n-1) (2) \[3pt]
 		& = -1 + 2n - 2 \[3pt]
		& = 2n - 3.
	}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: The fifth and sixth terms of an arithmetic sequence are $46$ and $50,$ respectively. Determine the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by 

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d,
$$

so we need to figure out the first term $a_1$ and the common difference $d.$

Since the terms $a_5=46$ and $a_6=50$ are consecutive, we can subtract them to find the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{6}-{a}_{5} \\  & =50-46 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, $a_5=46,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since $a_5$ is $4$ jumps after $a_1,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
a_5 &= a_1 + 4d \[3pt]
46 &= a_1 + 4\cdot 4\[3pt]
46 &= a_1 +16 \[3pt]
46-16 &= a_1\[3pt]
      a_1&= 30.
	}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence is

$$
\eqalign{
		a_n&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
 		& = 30 + (n-1) \cdot 4 \[3pt]
 		& =30 + 4n -4 \[3pt]
		& = 4n +26.
	}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Nth Term Given Two Non-Consecutive Terms
canonical_examples.problem: An arithmetic sequence has the $3$rd term $a_{3}=9$ and the $8$th term is $a_{8}=69.$ Find a formula for the $n$th term of the sequence.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term is given by  

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d,
$$

so we need to figure out what the first term $a_1$ and the common difference $d$ are.

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms $a_{8}=69$ and $a_{3}=9$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{8}-{a}_{3}}{8-3} \\  & =\frac{69-9}{8-3} \\  & =\frac{60}{5} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, $a_{3}=9,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since $a_{3}$ is $2$ jumps after $a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}+2d \\ 9 & ={a}_{1}+2\cdot 12 \\ 9 & ={a}_{1}+24 \\ {a}_{1} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-15+(n-1)\cdot 12 \\  & =-15+12n-12 \\  & =12n-27.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To find the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence given two arbitrary terms, we must usually apply the following:

- The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is given by

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d
$$

where $a_n$ is the $n$th term, $a_1$ is the first term, and $d$ is the common difference.

- We can find the common difference $d$ of an arithmetic sequence given two arbitrary terms using

$$
d = \frac{a_m-a_k}{m-k}
$$

where $a_m$ is the $m$th term, and $a_k$ is the $k$th term.

Let's see some examples.
